q: Under Ind AS 116, a contract contains a lease only if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset. Control requires the customer to have:
o: Legal title to the underlying asset throughout the whole contract term
An option to purchase the underlying asset at the end of the term
Physical possession of the underlying asset at all times in use
Substantially all the economic benefits and the right to direct use
why: Control is defined by the combination of obtaining substantially all economic benefits and directing how and for what purpose the asset is used. Title, possession, and purchase options are not the defining tests.

q: A supplier has a substantive substitution right over the asset throughout the period of use. The consequence under Ind AS 116 is:
o: The asset is identified, but the lease is classified as short-term
There is no identified asset, so the contract contains no lease
The customer still recognises a right-of-use asset at its fair value
The contract is treated as a service concession arrangement instead
why: A substantive substitution right, meaning the supplier has the practical ability to substitute and would benefit economically from doing so, means no identified asset and therefore no lease. A right that is only exercisable on malfunction or repair is not substantive.

q: The lease liability at commencement is measured at the present value of lease payments not yet paid, discounted using:
o: The incremental borrowing rate of the lessee in all circumstances
The risk free rate on government securities of a comparable tenure
The rate implicit in the lease if readily determinable, else IBR
The weighted average cost of capital of the lessee at commencement
why: Ind AS 116 requires the implicit rate where readily determinable, falling back to the incremental borrowing rate. Lessees commonly cannot determine the implicit rate because they do not know the unguaranteed residual value, which is why the IBR is used in practice.

q: Which of the following is NOT included in the initial measurement of the right-of-use asset?
o: Variable payments linked to future sales, not based on an index
Payments made at or before commencement, less incentives received
An estimate of dismantling and restoration costs to be incurred
Initial direct costs that have been incurred by the lessee itself
why: Variable payments linked to sales or usage are excluded from both the liability and the asset and are expensed as incurred. Payments varying with an index or rate are included, measured using the index at commencement.

q: The low value exemption in Ind AS 116 is applied:
o: By reference to the materiality level determined for the lessee
Only where the lessee also applies the short-term exemption to all leases
Only to leases whose term is shorter than a period of twelve months
Asset by asset, on the value of the asset when new, whatever lessee size
why: Low value is assessed on the absolute value of the underlying asset when new and is applied lease by lease, independent of the lessee size or materiality. The exemption is not available if the lessee subleases or expects to sublease the asset.

q: The short-term lease exemption is unavailable where:
o: The lease term is exactly twelve months and has no options
The lease contains a purchase option granted to the lessee
The lessor happens to be a related party of the lessee company
The underlying asset leased is a motor vehicle used by staff
why: A lease containing a purchase option cannot be a short-term lease under Ind AS 116, regardless of its term. A twelve month lease with no purchase option does qualify, and the exemption is an election by class of underlying asset.

q: A lease modification that increases the scope by adding the right to use an additional asset, with consideration increased by an amount commensurate with the stand-alone price for that increase, is accounted for as:
o: A remeasurement of the existing liability at a revised discount rate
A termination of the original lease and recognition of a new lease
A separate lease accounted for independently of the original lease
An immediate gain or loss recognised within profit or loss for the year
why: Both conditions being met, increased scope and commensurate price increase, requires the modification to be treated as a separate lease. Where the price increase is not commensurate, the existing liability is remeasured using a revised discount rate instead.

q: A lease modification decreases the scope of the lease. The lessee should:
o: Reduce the right-of-use asset proportionately and book a gain or loss
Adjust the right-of-use asset alone, with no gain or loss arising at all
Recognise the whole reduction in the lease liability as deferred income
Treat the reduction in scope as though it were a separate new lease
why: A scope decrease requires proportionate reduction of the right-of-use asset with any difference against the remeasured liability recognised in profit or loss. Deferring the effect misstates both the asset and the period result.

q: Under Ind AS 116, a lessor classifies a lease as a finance lease when:
o: The lease term covers more than 75 percent of the asset economic life
It transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership
The present value of lease payments exceeds 90 percent of fair value
Legal title to the asset passes at the end of the lease in all cases
why: Classification rests on whether substantially all risks and rewards of ownership transfer, assessed using indicators rather than bright lines. The 75 percent and 90 percent figures are US style bright lines and are not thresholds in Ind AS 116.

q: A lessee remeasures the lease liability using a REVISED discount rate when:
o: Payments alter because of a market rent review clause in the contract
The credit standing of the lessee entity improves during the term
The consumer price index used for escalation of the rent changes
The lease term changes, or the purchase option assessment changes
why: Changes in lease term or purchase option assessment require an unchanged cash flow pattern to be rediscounted at a revised rate. Index or rate driven payment changes are remeasured using the original discount rate, which is the common trap.

q: A ten year property lease has a market rent review after five years. At commencement the lessee should:
o: Use the rent in effect at commencement and remeasure on the review
Include estimated future market rent increases in the lease payments
Treat the whole lease as variable and expense the payments made
Recognise a provision now for the expected future rent increase
why: Market rent reviews are not based on an index or rate in the sense of a formula driven adjustment, so the lessee uses the rent in effect and remeasures when the change takes effect. Forecasting rent increases into the initial liability is not permitted.

q: Which audit procedure is MOST effective in addressing the completeness of the lease population under Ind AS 116?
o: Recomputing the discount unwind on leases already in the register
Confirming the lease terms with lessors already listed in the register
Scanning rent and hire expense accounts and reviewing board minutes
Agreeing the opening right-of-use asset to the prior year figure
why: Completeness risk lies with arrangements never entered in the register, so procedures must look outside it, such as scanning expense accounts and contract approvals. Testing items already in the register addresses accuracy but cannot detect omissions.

q: A sale and leaseback where the transfer does NOT qualify as a sale under Ind AS 115 should be accounted for by the seller-lessee as:
o: Derecognition of the asset and recognition of a right-of-use asset
A right-of-use asset at its fair value with the gain taken to OCI
A full gain on the sale and an operating lease expense taken thereafter
Continued recognition of the asset and a financial liability raised
why: If control does not transfer, no sale has occurred, so the asset stays on the balance sheet and the proceeds are a financial liability under Ind AS 109. Recognising a gain would be recognising profit on a financing transaction.

q: The lease term under Ind AS 116 comprises the non-cancellable period plus:
o: Every optional renewal period that is available to it under the contract
Optional periods where the reasonably certain test is met by the lessee
Any period for which the lessee has historically occupied premises
Renewal periods only where the lessor has no right to refuse them
why: Only options the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise, and termination options it is reasonably certain not to exercise, extend the lease term. Including all available options regardless of intent overstates both the asset and the liability.

q: A manufacturer dealer lessor enters a finance lease. At commencement it recognises:
o: Selling profit or loss as on an outright sale, plus finance income
Only finance income spread across the term of the finance lease
The asset at cost, depreciated over its estimated useful life
A right-of-use asset together with a matching lease liability raised
why: Manufacturer or dealer lessors recognise selling profit or loss at commencement, calculated using a market rate of interest, and then finance income over the term. Deferring all profit into finance income would misstate both revenue and margin.

q: Which characteristic would MOST support the conclusion that the customer directs the use of an identified asset?
o: The supplier operates the asset under its own protocols throughout
The underlying asset is physically located at the supplier premises
The customer decides what output is produced, when, and how much
The customer pays a fixed monthly fee for the use of the asset
why: Deciding the how and for what purpose of use during the period of use is the core of directing use. Location of the asset and the payment structure are not determinative, and supplier controlled operation with predetermined output points away from a lease.

q: A lessee elects the short-term exemption for a class of office equipment leases. It must:
o: Recognise a right-of-use asset but no corresponding lease liability at all
Capitalise the payments and amortise them over the asset expected life
Recognise a lease liability but no corresponding right-of-use asset
Expense the payments on a straight-line basis and disclose the election
why: The exemption results in straight-line recognition of the payments as expense, with specific disclosure of the election and expense amount. Partial recognition of only an asset or only a liability is not an option under the standard.

q: In auditing lease data, which input would ordinarily be the HIGHEST risk of material misstatement in the lease liability?
o: The monthly fixed rent that is stated in the executed lease contract
The incremental borrowing rate applied and the lease term assessed
The commencement date shown on the signed handover certificate
The currency in which the lease contract has been denominated
why: The discount rate and the lease term involve significant estimation and judgement and small changes materially shift the liability. Contractual rent and handover dates are objectively verifiable from documents and carry far less estimation risk.
